_meta.description: Cycle & innings — where each vertical sits in its structural growth cycle (1-9 innings), with structural-demand strength, capex under-investment, and business-cycle risk scored 0-100. Verdict is a quick read, not advice.

froth_monitor.headline: July 2026 delivered the first real froth-shakeout of this cycle: chip stocks shed over $1T of market cap in late July even as fundamentals printed records. Beats were sold (TSMC, ASML), misses were punished violently (Samsung, SK Hynix). The tape is repricing expectations, not demand — which is exactly when volatility hands you entries into structurally-tight chokepoints.
froth_monitor.stance: Selective-opportunistic. The froth signals are real (beat-and-raise inversion, hidden lease leverage, inference price deflation) but the demand spine is intact (~$700B of 2026 hyperscaler capex, revised UP $173B since January). Favor contractual chokepoint owners over names priced for perfection; treat >15% drawdowns in conviction-3 names as staggered-entry windows, not thesis breaks.

signals.d: TSMC Q2 (Jul 14): record $22B net profit, +77% y/y, EPS $4.31 vs $3.77 est, raised 2026 capex to $60–64B — and the stock FELL. ASML beat and fell too. The market now reads capex strength as a margin threat rather than a demand signal. Sentiment inversion on good news is a classic late-froth marker.

signals.t: Memory air-pocket: thesis intact, multiple compressed
signals.d: SK Hynix posted its worst Seoul session on record (Jul 13), then Q2 results (Jul 29, −9.6%): record ₩79.3T revenue, 76% operating margin — but HBM long-term agreements cap short-term price elasticity and HBM4 mass-production revenue slips to Q3. A record-margin oligopolist de-rating on contract structure, not demand, is the profile of a froth-driven entry.

2026 capex estimates for the top-5 US hyperscalers now ~$697B — revised UP $173B since January. TSMC raised its own build budget by ~$8B mid-year. Whatever the tape does, the physical build-out (fabs, packaging, power, optics) is still expanding.

signals.t: Hidden leverage: $662B of off-balance-sheet DC leases
signals.d: Moody's flags ~$662B of datacenter lease commitments signed but not yet commenced — sitting off balance sheet under GAAP. If AI monetization disappoints, this is where the credit stress surfaces first. Watch the DC REIT / neocloud layer, not the chipmakers.

signals.t: Inference price deflation squeezes GPU renters
signals.d: Cloud inference pricing per 1K tokens is down 30–40% since January; H200 spot instances are 20–25% cheaper than six months ago. Token deflation is great for AI adoption but compresses ROI for anyone renting out silicon — neoclouds and GPU resellers carry the margin risk, not the chokepoint suppliers.

Broadcom launched Thor Ultra networking silicon and signed a ~$10B custom-chip supply deal with OpenAI starting late 2026. The 'Carving Up the TPU' thesis — value migrating to ASIC co-design + the network — keeps getting external confirmation.

The Jul 16 selloff spread to power, cooling and electrical names on rotation flows, with no change in their fundamentals — the grid/cooling build-out remains the most supply-constrained layer of the stack. Meanwhile Corning is expanding US optical manufacturing ~10x backed by NVIDIA and Amazon commitments: optics demand is being contractually underwritten through the froth.

cycles.sum: The most defensible, least cyclical layer — royalty/license model that compounds with design starts. Well-invested (no supply gap). Main risk is valuation and the geopolitical on/off lever to China, not demand.

Structural beneficiary of every fab buildout, but WFE spend is lumpy and China-localization demand is rolling over. ASML and the deep subsystem chokepoints (Zeiss, VAT) are the durable holds; broad WFE is more cyclical.

Leading-edge demand is structural and supply is capital-constrained (years to add). TSMC compounds; mature-node faces China overcapacity. The keystone of the universe, carrying the Taiwan-concentration tail risk.

HBM is structurally tight and sold out, but memory is historically the most cyclical semi segment. July 2026 showed the new tension: long-term HBM agreements give volume visibility but cap price upside — SK Hynix printed a 76% operating margin and still sold off hard on the LTA structure. Oligopoly pricing power vs contract-capped elasticity.

Value is migrating from front-end to back-end as scaling slows. CoWoS, substrates and bonding tools are under-built vs demand. Early-mid innings of a multi-year capacity-build with high structural support.

Highest structural demand in the universe, but also the highest scrutiny: the whole stack hinges on hyperscaler capex ROI. Custom ASICs add a second growth vector. Mid-innings with elevated cycle/ROI risk.

The network increasingly gates cluster utilization, and content per cluster is rising. Broadcom + connectivity silicon (Astera, Credo) are the picks-and-shovels. Early-mid; tied to the same capex cycle as compute.

Power and cooling are the binding constraints and badly under-built — liquid cooling is at an inflection. Early innings with very high structural support; the deepest cross-link to the energy supply chain.

Optics content per GPU is scaling fast and EML lasers are a genuine chokepoint. CPO (2026) is a step-change ahead. Early innings; main risk is technology transitions (CPO/LPO) reshuffling the value chain.

Big structural promise (a whole new BOM) but highly speculative on timing and volume. Component chokepoints (reducers, screws) are the cleanest exposure. Very early innings — size positions to the uncertainty.

Rides both robotics and broader automation. Sony sensors and the Nvidia robot-brain are durable; force/torque and tactile sensing are an unsolved gap. Early innings with steadier non-humanoid demand underneath.

A make-or-break AR component with no clear winning technology yet — high risk, high optionality. Most leaders are private (JBD). Very early; the bet is on which display tech (microLED/OLEDoS/LCoS) scales.

Earliest-stage theme in the universe — full AR is years out and waveguide tech is unsettled. Meta's Ray-Ban breakout is the consumer on-ramp. Very early; component layer (glass, SoC) is more investable than device brands.
